title: Stack & queue problem practice
overview: A practice module with no new code: you use the stack and queue you already built to solve judge problems. The goal is to recognise when a problem is secretly a stack problem (matching, undo, most-recent-first) or a queue problem (first come, first served, rotating order). Solve the linked problems, then check the patterns below.

body: There is no new code today. Everything you need was built in Modules 13 and 14. What this day trains is one small decision you have to make before writing a single line: **is this a stack problem or a queue problem?**

Two everyday pictures answer it. A canteen counter has a pile of washed plates. New plates go on the top, and whoever needs a plate takes the top one, the plate put down last. A ticket window has a line of people. You join at the back, and the person served next is the one who has been waiting longest.
intro.trace:
pile of plates        ticket line

  [ D ]  <- take       A  B  C  D
  [ C ]                ^        ^
  [ B ]                serve    join
  [ A ]                here     here

body: So the question to ask a problem is: when the time comes to deal with something, is it the **newest** thing that must be dealt with, or the **oldest**? Newest first means a stack. Oldest first means a queue. Nothing else about the problem matters for this choice.

**First worked example.** Check that the brackets in `( [ ] )` are balanced. You read `]`. Which opening bracket is it supposed to close? Not the first one you saw, but the most recent one still waiting, which is `[`. The last thing seen has to be dealt with first, so the waiting brackets belong on a stack.
intro.trace:
string:  ( [ ] )

read (   push        stack: (
read [   push        stack: ( [
read ]   top is [ -> pop     stack: (
read )   top is ( -> pop     stack: empty

stack empty at the end  ->  balanced

body: Notice what the stack saved you. Without it, for every closing bracket you would walk backwards through the string hunting for the nearest opening bracket that is still unmatched. That is a loop inside a loop: O(n²), which on a string of 100000 characters is about 10,000,000,000 steps and will not finish in a second. With a stack every character is pushed at most once and popped at most once, so the whole scan is O(n).

**Second worked example**, this time with arrival order. A queue holds `1 2 3 4 5` and you must reverse only the first 3. Pour those 3 through a stack, because a stack hands them back in the opposite order, then rotate the untouched 2 items from the front to the back so they end up behind again.
intro.trace:
queue: 1 2 3 4 5      k = 3

pop 3 into a stack    stack: 3 2 1  (top first)
                      queue: 4 5
push them back        queue: 4 5 3 2 1
rotate 5 - 3 = 2      queue: 5 3 2 1 4
  front to back       queue: 3 2 1 4 5

body: Three patterns cover most of the linked problems. **Matching and cancelling**: push each character, and pop instead of pushing when the new one cancels the top. Brackets work this way, and so do backspaces and removing adjacent duplicates. For `abbaca` the stack goes `a`, `ab`, then the second `b` cancels the `b`, the next `a` cancels the `a`, so `c` and `a` are pushed and `ca` is what is left.

**Next greater element**: for every number, find the first larger number to its right. Comparing every pair is O(n²). Instead walk from right to left with a stack holding only the numbers that could still be somebody's answer: pop everything not larger than the current value, and what is left on top is the answer.

**Simulation with a queue**: when the problem describes people or jobs arriving and being handled in order, act the story out. Join at the back with `push`, serve the front with `front()` and `pop()`, and send someone to the back of the line by popping and pushing the same value.
intro.snippet:
if(!st.empty() && st.top() == c) st.pop();
else st.push(c);

body: Two habits save most of the wrong answers here. Always check `empty()` before `top()`, `front()` or `pop()`, because reading the top of an empty stack is not an error message, it is undefined behaviour. And remember the stack only lets you touch the top: to reach the bottom, or to keep a running minimum, you need a second stack or a recursive call to hold the rest while you work.
The concepts below name each pattern with its snippet, and the practice links are the problems to try. Decide plates or ticket line first, and the code usually follows in a few lines.

concepts.explain: A stack only lets you touch the top. Use it when the newest item must be handled first, like the last opened bracket or the last typed character.
Push every opening bracket. On a closing bracket, the top must be its partner; if the stack is empty or the top does not match, the string is invalid. At the end the stack must be empty.
For problems like 'backspace' or 'remove adjacent duplicates', push characters and pop when the new character cancels the top. What is left in the stack is the final string (read it bottom to top).

Pouring a queue into a stack and back reverses it, because the stack gives items back in the opposite order. To reverse only the first k items, pour k items through a stack, then rotate the remaining n-k items to the back.

concepts.term: Inserting at the bottom of a stack
concepts.explain: You cannot reach the bottom directly. Pop everything into a helper (another stack or recursion), push the new value, then push everything back.
Keep a second stack that stores the minimum so far at every level. Push `min(x, minStack.top())` together with each push, and pop both together, so `getMin` is O(1).
A queue adds at the back and removes at the front. Use it when order of arrival matters, or to rotate items (pop from front, push to back).

practice_links.name: Insert An Element At Its Bottom In A Given Stack
Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String
Reverse First K Elements of Queue

recap: Newest-first or 'cancel the last thing' problems are stack problems.
Arrival-order or rotation problems are queue problems.
A stack reverses order; use that to reverse a queue or part of it.
A second stack of running minimums gives O(1) `getMin`.

check_yourself.q: For the string `([)]`, at which character does the bracket check fail, and why?
check_yourself.a: At `)`: the top of the stack is `[`, which is not the partner of `)`.

check_yourself.q: Why is a string like `((` invalid even though no mismatch happens?
check_yourself.a: Because the stack is not empty at the end; two brackets were never closed.

check_yourself.q: You push 5, 3, 7 into a min stack. What does the helper stack hold, bottom to top?
check_yourself.a: 5, 3, 3 — each level stores the smallest value seen so far.

check_yourself.q: How do you reverse only the first k items of a queue of size n?
check_yourself.a: Pop k items into a stack, push them back into the queue (now reversed at the back), then move the front n-k items to the back once each.

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: reversing the first 3 of `1 2 3 4 5`
body: The second worked example above, step by step. The queue is drawn front-first, the stack bottom-first, so the end each structure is used at is marked with a `^`.
There are three separate phases and it helps to name them as they go past: pour the first three into a stack, pour the stack back, then rotate the untouched values round to the back.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows or Play to follow all three phases

frames.label: The queue holds `1 2 3 4 5`. Only the first three must be reversed; 4 and 5 have to end up behind them, still in their own order.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  1 2 3 4 5
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

frames.label: Phase one. Take the front value off the queue and push it on the stack. 1 leaves the queue, 1 lands on the stack.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  2 3 4 5
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  1
                      ^ top

frames.label: Take 2 the same way. It goes **on top of** 1, which is the whole point - the stack is storing them upside down.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  3 4 5
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  1 2
                        ^ top

frames.label: And 3. The first three values are now all on the stack with 3 on top, and the queue holds only the part we must not disturb.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  4 5
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  1 2 3
                          ^ top

frames.label: Phase two: pour the stack back. `top()` is 3, so 3 is the first one to rejoin the queue - and it joins at the **back**, behind 4 and 5.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  4 5 3
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  1 2
                        ^ top

frames.label: Then 2, which is now the top.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  4 5 3 2
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  1
                      ^ top

frames.label: Then 1 last of all. The first three are reversed - but they are sitting at the back of the line, which is not where they belong.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  4 5 3 2 1
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

frames.label: Phase three: rotate. Pop the front value 4 and push it straight back on. Nothing is lost; the line just turns round by one place.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  5 3 2 1 4
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

frames.label: Rotate the second untouched value, 5, the same way, and it is done: `3 2 1 4 5`. The number of rotations is `n - k`, here 5 - 3 = 2, which is exactly how many values were never meant to move.
frames.art:
k = 3:  reverse the first three, leave the rest

queue front -> back:  3 2 1 4 5
                      ^ front

stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

walkthrough.heading: Watch it happen: cancelling the pairs in `abbaca`
body: The same stack, a different question: remove every pair of equal letters that stand next to each other, and keep going while removing one pair creates another.
The rule in the snippet above is the whole program: if the new letter equals the top of the stack, pop instead of pushing. Watch the stack hold the letters that have survived so far.
walkthrough.frames_title: Press the arrows to read the word one letter at a time

frames.label: Reading `abbaca` left to right. The stack will hold every letter that has not been cancelled yet, in order, so its top is always the letter immediately to the left of where we are.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a


stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

frames.label: Read `a`. The stack is empty, so there is nothing for it to cancel with. Push it.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
          ^ push

stack bottom -> top:  a

frames.label: Read `b`. The top is `a`, which is different, so this is not a pair. Push `b` on top.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
            ^ top is a - different, push

stack bottom -> top:  a b
                        ^ top

frames.label: Read the second `b`. The top **is** `b`, so these two are a neighbouring pair: pop the top and do not push the new one. Both are gone at once.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
              ^ top was b - pop, both go

stack bottom -> top:  a

frames.label: Read `a`. Removing the two b's has made this `a` a neighbour of the first `a`, and the stack already knew: its top is `a`. Pop, and that pair goes too.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
                ^ top was a - pop, both go

stack bottom -> top:  (empty)

frames.label: Read `c`. The stack is empty again, so `c` has no neighbour on its left. Push it.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
                  ^ push

stack bottom -> top:  c

frames.label: Read the last `a`. The top is `c`, which is different, so push. Nothing left to cancel.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a
                    ^ top is c - different, push

stack bottom -> top:  c a
                        ^ top

frames.label: The word is finished, so read the stack from the bottom up: `ca`. Every letter was pushed at most once and popped at most once, so one single pass does the whole job - and the stack found the chain reaction in the middle without ever looking backwards.
frames.art:
string:   a b b a c a


stack bottom -> top:  c a
                        ^ top
